title: How do you solve an M&A case from start to finish, with a fully worked example?
description: The complete M&A case guide: standalone value, synergies, integration cost and price, worked through a $60M bakery acquisition, plus mistakes and practice.
hook: You solve an M&A case by comparing what the target is worth to your client with the price being asked: its value on its own, plus the synergies your client can realistically deliver, minus the cost of integrating it. If that total beats the price, and buying beats the alternatives, the deal makes sense. This guide works through a $60M bakery acquisition and shows how one assumption can flip the answer.
body:
In this guide

  • When you will meet an M&A case
  • The structure, and the first question to ask
  • A fully worked example: a $60M bakery deal
  • Two refinements that separate strong candidates
  • Strong and weak answers
  • The mistakes that cost candidates this case
  • Practise with these prompts
  • Where to practise next

When you will meet an M&A case

A company is thinking about buying another company, merging with one, or buying a stake. The prompt is usually "should our client buy X?", sometimes "what is X worth?" or "what is the most we should pay?" Private equity cases use much of the same logic, but a fund has no existing business to create synergies with, so the value has to come from growth, efficiency and the eventual sale.

The structure, and the first question to ask

Start with the rationale, because it tells you what the deal has to deliver:

Why does the client want to buy: growth, a capability, cost savings or access to a new market?

Then work through four questions:

  • Is the target good on its own? Its market, its performance against peers, and its standalone value from multiples or a DCF.
  • What extra is it worth to us? Cost synergies, revenue synergies, minus one-off integration costs.
  • Can we make it work? Funding, integration and culture, and competition regulators.
  • Is the price right? Price against value to us, and against alternatives: another target, building it ourselves or partnering.

The decision rule fits on one line: buy only if standalone value + synergies − integration costs is more than the price, and buying beats the alternatives. The acquisition framework explains each branch in more depth.

A fully worked example: a $60M bakery deal

The prompt: a regional bakery chain can buy a smaller rival for $60M. Should it? The numbers are illustrative.

Step 1: standalone value

The rival makes $5M of operating profit a year. Similar businesses sell for about 10 times operating profit, so it is worth about $50M on its own. The asking price is already $10M above that, so the client would be paying $10M for synergies before it has delivered any.

Step 2: synergies

Sharing bakeries, buying flour together and merging head-office roles could save $2M a year. Valued on the same basis as the target (10 times operating profit), that is worth $20M.

Step 3: integration cost

Merging IT systems, closing one bakery and paying redundancies costs about $6M, once.

Step 4: value to us against price

$50M + $20M − $6M = $64M, against a $60M price. The deal creates value, but only $4M of it.

Step 5: test the risk

Synergies are the assumption most likely to disappoint, so test them. If only half arrive ($1M a year, worth $10M), value is $50M + $10M − $6M = $54M, below the price. Work out the break-even instead of guessing: the client needs synergies worth $60M − $50M + $6M = $16M, which is $1.6M a year, or 80% of the plan.

Step 6: the recommendation

I'd recommend buying, but not at $60M without protection. Standalone, the rival is worth about $50M, so at $60M we are paying for savings we have to create ourselves, and we break even only if we deliver 80% of the $2M plan. I'd push the price towards $55M, where we would need just 55% of the savings, or pay part of the price as an earn-out. Before signing, I'd plan the bakery consolidation in detail, because that is where most of the savings sit.

Check the $55M figure: $55M − $50M + $6M = $11M of synergy value needed, which is $1.1M a year, or 55% of $2M.

Two refinements that separate strong candidates

Ask what the price includes

A multiple of operating profit or EBITDA values the whole business, its enterprise value. Shareholders receive that value minus debt plus spare cash. So ask whether the $60M is for the shares or for the whole business. If the rival also has $8M of bank debt the buyer must repay, the real cost is $68M, against $64M of value, and the deal destroys value from day one.

Keep annual figures and valuations apart

Never add an annual saving straight to a valuation: $2M a year and $50M of value are different units. Convert the saving into a value first, and do it on the same basis as the target. Here both the target and the savings are valued on operating profit. If the multiple were on after-tax profit, you would first take tax off the savings, which shrinks their value.

Finally, think about who keeps the synergy. If rival bidders push the price up to the full $64M, the seller captures all the value and the buyer gains nothing for taking the integration risk.

Strong and weak answers

A weak answer values the target and stops:

It earns $5M at a 10x multiple, so it's worth $50M. That seems like a good business.

A strong answer compares value with price and finds the swing factor:

Standalone, it's worth about $50M, so at $60M we are paying $10M for synergies. Let's see if they are worth more than that.
The answer hinges on synergies: at half the savings, the deal destroys value.

The mistakes that cost candidates this case

  1. Valuing the target and never comparing it with the price. The question is always value to us against price.
  2. Counting synergies but forgetting integration. Integration costs are one-off but real, and they arrive before the savings.
  3. Taking synergies at face value. Run the "half the savings" test and work out the break-even.
  4. Ignoring alternatives. Could the client build the capability, partner, or buy a cheaper target?
  5. Forgetting non-financial risks. Culture, key staff leaving, customers defecting and competition approval can each sink a deal that works on paper.

Practise with these prompts

Quick maths: a target earns $8M of EBITDA and peers trade at 7x EBITDA. It has $10M of debt and $4M of spare cash. What is its equity value?

Show the answer

Enterprise value = $8M × 7 = $56M. Equity value = $56M − $10M debt + $4M cash = $50M. If the seller asks $56M for the shares, you would overpay by $6M, because you also take on $10M of debt and get only $4M of cash.

How would you value a football club for a potential buyer?

Show the answer
  • Revenue: media rights, match-day and commercial income; which are contracted and which are at risk from relegation.
  • Costs: player wages and transfers, stadium and staff; net debt and the value of the squad.
  • Value methods: multiples from recent club deals, and a cash-flow value.
  • Strategic premium: brand, stadium, land, and what this buyer can add.

Where to start: revenue and how safe it is, because media money depends on staying in the league.

The trap: using one method only; club deals rarely match cash-flow values.

Should a coffee chain buy its main coffee roaster?

Show the answer
  • Value of the roaster: its profits and other customers; price against value.
  • Benefits to us: cheaper beans, security of supply, quality control.
  • Risks: the roaster's other customers (often rivals) may leave; running a factory is a new skill.
  • Alternatives: a long-term supply contract or a minority stake.

Where to start: alternatives. A long contract may give most of the benefit without buying.

The trap: assuming ownership is the only way to secure supply.

Where to practise next

  • Run a full case: PackRight (a packaging maker eyeing a plastics recycler) or Tidewell Foods (is a healthy-snack brand worth $110M to us?).
  • Revise the opening: what to ask first in an M&A case, and the trap.
  • Brush up on valuation: payback and NPV, step by step.
  • More prompts: 16 M&A, strategy and new business questions.
